title: Votes at 16: Making the First Election Count
label: 9 September 2026 · Lowering the voting age
summary: MPs examined how the UK could extend voting rights to 16 and 17-year-olds, drawing on experience in Scotland and Wales. Election officials warned that changing the law isn't enough: young people must be registered, understand how to vote and have suitable identification, while councils need time and resources to prepare. Education and youth organisations strongly supported lowering the voting age, arguing that young people are capable of making political choices and deserve a say in decisions affecting their lives. However, witnesses acknowledged that access to voting remains unequal, and there is limited evidence about whether votes at 16 have changed election results. The discussion explored automatic registration, practical voting lessons, political education, online misinformation and how politicians can better engage young people. The broad message from witnesses was that lowering the voting age offers opportunities, but its success depends heavily on preparation, education and sustained engagement.

chapters.title: 1. Lessons from Scotland and Wales
chapters.takeaway: Introducing votes at 16 works best when election officials have plenty of preparation time and young people receive clear information before their first election.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Scotland and Wales already allow 16 and 17-year-olds to vote in certain elections. What should England and Northern Ireland learn from their experience?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Wales gave itself quite a long preparation period. Young people could start registering in June 2020, ahead of the Senedd election in May 2021. We could register people from age 14 and explain that they would be able to vote from 16. We used a national leaflet and follow-up letters to households. Covid restricted our work in schools and communities, but that preparation helped.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Scotland first allowed 16 and 17-year-olds to vote in the 2014 independence referendum. We spent around 11 months identifying and registering young people, using household forms and information from schools. The referendum attracted enormous publicity, which helped people understand that voting rights were changing. Election officials also worked with schools to explain the process.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: How did you help young people understand what actually happens when they go to vote?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Councils made videos showing someone entering a polling station, approaching the desk and receiving their ballot paper. That helped remove the uncertainty. Once Covid restrictions eased, we did more work with youth groups and community organisations. It wasn't just about getting young people registered. We wanted them to understand why voting matters and feel confident doing it.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: Did you find out whether those activities actually worked?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Feedback from projects in Swansea was very positive. Swansea appointed two pupils from each secondary school area as voting ambassadors to encourage their classmates to register and participate. Other councils tried similar schemes. I wish we'd had a national programme to support them. Across Wales, registration numbers rose substantially between the 2021 and 2022 elections. In Powys, the increase was around 80%. That followed much more extensive engagement work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The proposed changes would also make the voting age consistent across different elections. Would that help?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Definitely. At the moment, young people can vote in some elections but not others. That's confusing. A single voting age would make registration campaigns and conversations with young people much clearer.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: What's the minimum time needed between changing the law and introducing votes at 16 in a UK general election?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: I'd regard six months as an absolute minimum, and practical arrangements might require longer. The Electoral Commission recommended at least six months between the Scottish law being approved and the start of registration preparations. There's also the Gould principle, which warns against changing election law within six months of an election. We must be particularly careful because general elections don't have fixed dates. Rushing a change risks mistakes that could damage public confidence.

chapters.title: 2. Who Gets Left Out?
chapters.takeaway: Younger voters face different obstacles, particularly when their families are disengaged or the registration system doesn't fit their circumstances.

turns.speaker: Sarah Smith
turns.text: What are the main barriers preventing young people from voting?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Registration is the first challenge. If voting starts at 16, we need to reach people from age 14 so they're ready. Parents can be a barrier because they often control a young person's contact with official organisations. Some parents think their children aren't mature enough to register. Some young people feel that way themselves. Schools, community groups and people they trust can help them make their own informed decision.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Registration is much lower among younger people than older adults. What have you learned about reaching different groups?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: We mustn't treat young people as one identical group. They have different backgrounds, disabilities, languages and living arrangements. We use education records to identify potential voters and invite them to register, but those records aren't always up to date. Someone splitting their time between two homes, for example, can face difficulties deciding where to register. We need arrangements that work for different circumstances.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Young people whose parents already vote are generally easier to reach because their families encourage them. Other families have little connection with politics. Some young people don't see how political decisions affect their lives. That's where properly funded staff visiting schools, youth groups and community organisations can make a difference.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Have you worked with particular communities to reach people who might otherwise miss out?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: There have been different projects involving schools and community organisations, but they haven't always continued consistently. A major election can generate a lot of publicity and interest, but we also need ongoing engagement. In Scotland, recent Electoral Commission figures suggest only around 60% of 16 and 17-year-olds are registered, slightly below earlier levels. There's still considerable room for improvement.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: Have you seen evidence that allowing 16 and 17-year-olds to vote actually changed an election result or increased turnout?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: I can't say that it has clearly changed results or turnout. Wales introduced it during Covid, when our engagement work wasn't as extensive as we'd hoped. Awareness has improved, but people still contact us because they didn't realise 16-year-olds could vote. It's difficult to separate the impact of the voting-age change from everything else happening in politics.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: I'm not qualified to judge whether election results have changed. I focus on making sure eligible people can register and vote. I also wouldn't assume that everyone who's registered is already interested in politics. When I visited schools, young people were interested in matters such as public transport and car insurance costs. They could see how political decisions affected their lives, even if they didn't think of themselves as politically active.

chapters.title: 3. Registration, Identity Checks and Practical Risks
chapters.takeaway: Automatic registration can bring more people onto the voting list, but checking records, meeting identification rules and managing large elections remain difficult.

turns.speaker: Sarah Smith
turns.text: What about voter identification? Young people may not have the documents needed to vote.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: That's another reason to allow plenty of preparation time. Young people need to know that registering isn't necessarily enough. If they're voting at a polling station where photographic ID is required, they need an accepted document or a free Voter Authority Certificate. We should consider whether the accepted documents include the forms of ID young people actually possess. Otherwise, someone might be registered but still unable to vote.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Powys took part in a trial of automatic voter registration. How did that work?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: We used existing council records, including education information, to identify eligible people who weren't registered. Where the information was sufficiently reliable, we could register them and send a notification. We identified just over 3,000 young people aged 14 to 18. Interestingly, none of the responses to that mailing came directly from young people. Parents contacted us instead, often worried that their child's details would appear on a public register.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Once we explained the privacy arrangements, those concerns generally eased. Some parents also asked how their children would learn to vote. The trial helped us register people, but it wasn't as closely connected to wider education activities as it could have been. We added more than 5,000 people overall in Powys, which had an electorate of around 106,000, but I can't point to a corresponding major increase in turnout.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: How much extra work did automatic registration create? Could councils manage it permanently?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: It was more work than I'd expected. We had to check information from council departments that collect data for completely different purposes. Once we'd confirmed someone's identity, the registration process was relatively straightforward, and only about 0.5% of those automatically registered opted out. But many records suggested someone might be eligible without proving it. We then had to investigate and contact those people. That takes time, money and staff with specialist data skills.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Could this encourage other council departments to improve the quality of their records?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: I think so. For example, some council tax records lacked a reliable property reference number, making it harder to check whether someone lived at the right address. Some disability parking permit records lacked full names or addresses because those details weren't needed for that service. If councils establish consistent standards, that would help. I hope much of the initial work won't need repeating every year, but automatic registration certainly isn't effortless for election staff.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: We must also remember that identity checks happen at several stages, not just at polling stations. People applying for postal votes undergo checks against government records. Around 5% fail those checks and have to supply other evidence, such as a passport, driving licence or a combination of other documents. Some young people won't have these. We should examine whether those requirements are suitable for them.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: But councils can issue free photographic identification. Doesn't that solve the problem?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Not for postal voting. The Voter Authority Certificate is for identification at a polling station. Postal vote applications have separate rules. When registering someone, I can sometimes verify their identity using education records. If their postal vote identity check fails, I can't use those same records in that way. That's an important distinction.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: Would it be safer to introduce votes at 16 in local elections first, so councils have time to prepare before a general election?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: The important thing isn't necessarily which election comes first. It's having enough time for registration, education and administration. Ideally, councils would complete an annual canvass, identify new voters and then build engagement activities towards an election the following May. A general election creates particular risks because of the sheer number of voters. If young people are promised a vote but can't register in time, or their postal applications can't be approved, we could lose their trust.

chapters.title: 4. Are 16-Year-Olds Ready to Vote?
chapters.takeaway: The education and youth experts supported lowering the voting age, arguing that research doesn't show young people are less capable of choosing representatives than adults.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Most public opinion polling suggests people oppose lowering the voting age. Why do you think now is the right time?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: I'd ask, if not now, when? Young people have campaigned for this for years. The UK Youth Parliament repeatedly made votes at 16 its leading campaign issue. Politics affects almost everything in their lives, and they understand that, even if they don't know every detail of government. I've worked with young people for more than 30 years, and this has been a consistent concern.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: I agree. Young people are willing and able to participate. I've spent over 30 years teaching them. Decisions made today will affect them for a long time, so they should have an opportunity to influence those decisions.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Public opinion can change quickly. In Scotland, support for votes at 16 grew after the change was introduced, and a majority now support the lower voting age. People saw that the feared problems didn't materialise. I would expect attitudes elsewhere in the UK to change in a similar way, although that's a prediction.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Critics argue that 16 and 17-year-olds don't have the knowledge or maturity to make sensible voting decisions. What does the research show?

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Researchers have tested how well young people identify parties and candidates that represent their interests. They haven't found significant differences between people aged 14 to 17 and the wider population. On those measures, young people are just as good, or just as bad, at choosing representatives who match their views as older voters.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: We don't require adults to prove that they're sufficiently knowledgeable or mature before voting, so applying that test only to young people seems unfair. The important thing is giving them the information and skills to make decisions. Political parties often direct their messages towards older voters because they're more likely to turn out. That needs to change.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Wales had a difficult introduction because of Covid, but even there we haven't seen evidence of a major collapse in turnout or trust in democracy. Research from Scotland and other countries also suggests that lowering the voting age needn't cause the problems critics fear. It can create opportunities to increase participation, especially when combined with good education and meaningful contact with politicians.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: We need to support young people before, during and after their first election. Mock elections are particularly useful because they let people practise voting, examine candidates' promises and understand what happens at a polling station. We also need to make sure young people with disabilities or additional support needs aren't excluded. A bad first experience could discourage someone from voting again.

chapters.title: 5. Learning How Democracy Works
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses wanted practical political education, better-trained teachers and support outside school so that family background doesn't determine who participates.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: What changes to the school curriculum would best prepare young people to vote?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: We need good citizenship education from primary school throughout secondary school, rather than suddenly introducing it when pupils are almost old enough to vote. There should be dedicated lessons taught by trained teachers. That requires investment in teacher training, both for new teachers and those already working in schools.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Schools should also be encouraged to offer citizenship qualifications. Changes to how secondary schools are assessed could give the subject greater importance. Ofsted inspections should check that pupils actually receive the education they're entitled to. Simply adding citizenship to the curriculum won't guarantee that it's taught well.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: Schools have crowded timetables. Couldn't political education be included in subjects like maths or physics, using election results and voting statistics as examples?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Those examples can help, and I work with teachers in other subjects to plan them. But citizenship also needs its own lessons. If we scatter it across the timetable, it risks losing its importance. Students need proper time to understand democracy, examine political arguments and practise discussing issues respectfully.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Schools matter, but young people spend around 85% of their waking hours outside them. Depending on the age group, around 18% to 27% are persistently absent from school. We can't reach everyone through classrooms alone. Youth workers need to provide practical learning too, and that work should connect with what schools teach. Young people learn more when they can see how something relates to their own lives.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Young people particularly want opportunities to discuss political issues and develop their own opinions. Teachers need clear guidance so they can lead those conversations without promoting a political party. Germany and Austria offer examples of guidance for discussing politics in schools. Estonia has developed nationally applicable guidance with young people's involvement. We could learn from those approaches.

turns.speaker: Sarah Smith
turns.text: Children whose parents already vote seem much more likely to register themselves. Could lowering the voting age actually widen the gap between families who participate in politics and those who don't?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: That's a genuine concern. Some families have little history of engaging with public institutions. Youth workers can reach young people beyond the family home, run mock elections and create opportunities to discuss political questions. We also work with parents and grandparents, so those conversations can influence whole families. But it needs consistent support, not just a short campaign before an election.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: The UK already has substantial inequalities in who votes. But lowering the age could help reduce them because more 16 and 17-year-olds are still in education, where we can reach them. Scottish research has found smaller differences in participation between social backgrounds at 16 and 17, with relatively higher participation among disadvantaged young people. We don't yet know exactly why. Still, it's an important opportunity.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: We shouldn't leave good political education to chance depending on which school someone attends. In my schools, we run mock general elections. Pupils read party manifestos, question candidates, listen to different viewpoints and compare their own results with the real election. Students from a wide range of backgrounds get involved. These activities teach them how to disagree respectfully and make decisions for themselves.

chapters.title: 6. Misinformation, Social Media and AI
chapters.takeaway: Young voters need help judging online information, but witnesses disagreed with treating misinformation as a problem unique to young people.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Research suggests younger people often encounter political misinformation online, and only about half of 13 to 17-year-olds feel confident distinguishing true information from false claims. Does lowering the voting age make media literacy more important?

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Yes, but misinformation affects everyone. Young people may report encountering it more often partly because they spend more time online and may be better at recognising suspicious material. They need trustworthy sources they can turn to. But adults aged 20 to 70 and beyond face the same problem, and many of them won't receive formal education about it.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: So you're suggesting young people may be better at recognising misinformation, rather than necessarily being more vulnerable to it?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: It's essential to teach students how to check sources, compare different accounts and recognise the difference between facts and opinions. One of my students recently warned me that something she'd read came from Reddit and she hadn't verified it yet. That's exactly the habit we want. My pupils regularly ask me where I've got a news story from. We should teach these skills to teachers and parents as well as young people.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Are teachers across the country receiving enough training to do this properly?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Not consistently. Some school groups provide excellent training, but others don't. Media literacy is becoming a stronger part of citizenship education, and teachers need practical support to deliver it. That should begin during teacher training and continue throughout their careers. It also matters for teachers of other subjects who face difficult political discussions in their classrooms.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: The technology creates further problems. Young people can use VPNs to make social media platforms think they're in another country, which affects the information they see. I don't think the Online Safety Act is working effectively for them. I'm also worried about AI chatbots. Young people ask these systems political questions, and answers can sound authoritative even when they're wrong. The technology is changing faster than educators can keep up.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: We also oppose banning young people from social media, because that could push them towards less visible parts of the internet. I'd rather equip them to question what they see and give them trusted adults to discuss it with. My nephew brings questionable online claims to me, but not every young person has someone available to help.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Do we have evidence about AI chatbots influencing which political parties young people support?

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: I'm not aware of evidence that answers that question. The technology is moving very quickly, and research struggles to keep pace. It's also difficult to conduct reliable studies involving relatively small groups of 16 and 17-year-olds. We should take the issue seriously, but we shouldn't claim to know things the evidence hasn't established.

chapters.title: 7. What Politicians and Schools Should Do Next
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses called for clearer communication from political parties, safe political discussion in schools and practical help for every new voter.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: What should political parties do to engage young people? And are teachers confident enough to discuss party politics in classrooms without appearing biased? Young people have told us they learn about government but not always what the different parties actually stand for. I support votes at 16, but I think it needs proper educational support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I should make clear that support for votes at 16 isn't a unanimous position of this Committee.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Youth workers are well placed to have those conversations because young people trust them. But they need clear rules about discussing politics without imposing their own opinions. We're preparing guidance for youth workers on that. Youth councils and the UK Youth Parliament already offer useful examples of young people standing for election, questioning candidates and practising voting.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Political parties aren't doing enough to communicate with young people. Many don't understand the parties' policies because those messages aren't reaching them. Parties should explain their ideas in accessible language, use the platforms young people actually use and produce more useful video content. At a recent UK Youth Parliament conference, many participants told me they didn't know what the main parties were trying to achieve.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Politicians should engage with young people throughout the year, not just when they want votes. Make manifestos easier to read. Visit schools regularly. In some projects in Germany, young people have helped politicians create social media content. Most importantly, listen to what young people say, take action where appropriate and then tell them what happened. Many young people don't participate because they believe nobody listens.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: My local MP, Stephen Morgan, regularly visits my school, speaks with students and listens to their concerns. We've also arranged online conversations with members of Parliament, so young people can participate without travelling to London. These opportunities make politics more real. I'd encourage MPs to work with schools and youth councils in their own areas.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: But are teachers equipped to discuss party politics fairly? And will parents accept those conversations taking place in school?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: The teachers I work with are confident because they receive training on controversial issues, classroom debate and political impartiality. That isn't true everywhere. We need better national training and clear guidance. We should also explain to parents how these lessons work. Teaching about political parties is entirely appropriate if teachers help students examine different views without telling them what to believe.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: One quick question: can votes at 16 succeed without automatic voter registration?

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Yes, it can.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Yes, it can.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Yes, it can.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: Finally, if you could each recommend one practical change to help newly eligible young people participate, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Run mock elections and practical voting exercises. Young people should know what they'll experience before they enter a real polling station.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Guarantee access to high-quality citizenship education, including those practical experiences, and invest in training the teachers who provide it.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Provide assisted voter registration so young people get help signing up, while we wait for automatic voter registration.
